Entries are now open for the following Spring Series reports:

Chardonnay
Cabernet Sauvignon
Cape Bordeaux Red Blends

title: Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape
summary:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation. “The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The post Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape appeared first on winemag.
content:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation.

Chris Williams of The Foundry.

“The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The day is vibrantly hot, the surrounding technicolor buildings of De Waterkant seem to pulse in its brightness. It’s the new vintage-release and the label’s cold viognier is the perfect counterpoint to the weather.

The Foundry “was born very much out of the impact that the Rhône made on me as a young winemaker travelling in 1994”. Established in an old shed at Joostenberg while Williams was at Meerlust, he left in 2020 to focus on the brand full-time.

“It looks like it was a plan,” he says of the five Rhône-style wines we are about to taste. “It wasn’t. The first vintage [2001] was a mishmash of varieties, but the syrah really stood out.” In 2004, he started co-fermenting syrah with viognier. “I liked the gloss, but not the sweetness and overt florals.” Instead, viognier became The Foundry’s second wine and its first white.

“The range evolved organically.” Part of this is the Cape’s suitability. “There are a lot of similarities with the Rhône,” he says, citing granite soils, a Mediterranean climate, windy summers and cold, wet winters. Crucially, says Williams, “they retain their flavour and acidity.”

White masquerading as red

The Viognier 2024 comes from a vineyard six kilometres from False Bay. At 13 per cent alcohol, it is linear, floral and restrained, with less opulence than typical examples. It’s the only wine made entirely in oak: “Terracotta took away too much of the variety’s perfume.”

We move on to the Grenache Blanc 2022 (Williams says it benefits from bottle age). He points out that few places in the world produce a single varietal. “It’s a very Cape style of wine.” By contrast, some examples he’s tasted in southern France and Spain are “actually quite dull”, where the grape is often used for volume and alcohol.

The grapes come primarily from his own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard with the rest from neighbouring grower Willie Mostert. Williams south-facing block ripens about a week later than Mostert’s sunnier, east-facing vineyard. Each vineyard is split into three cuvées: barrel, stainless steel and terracotta. “What makes it so interesting, both red and white, is the mouthfeel,” he posits. “You get this textural pithiness on the mid-palate after the fruit explosion on entry.”

That component is what draws him to the whites. “They’re thick-skinned because they’ve evolved to deal with the harsh climate of the southern Rhône.” The Foundry whites all have varying degrees of grip balanced by fruit and fresh acidity.

With the Roussanne 2024 now in glass, he points out its gold colour, due to its phenolic character. “I’m careful to balance the natural tannin with roussanne’s generous fruit.” Its skin-to-juice ratio yields just 500 litres per tonne from his Voor-Paardeberg vineyard. “Squish a grape and basically a blob of pulp with four seeds comes out.”

The 2024 is perfumed with incense, turmeric, and Chinese five-spice, offset by savouriness and lemony acidity. Fermented equally in terracotta and barrel, it needs oxygen “to really unlock these exotic flavours”.

“I’ve referred to it, usually after a bottle or two, as red wine in drag.” Roussanne, he adds, has incredible ageing potential, noting that his first vintage was 2010 and “that wine is only now fully mature”. One of his favourite wines, he says, is Château de Beaucastel’s Roussanne Vieilles Vignes, which “is just indestructible”.

Fresh and focused reds

“The inclusion of whole bunch is dependent on the stems,” says Williams, answering a question about the Grenache Noir 2022. “Too green, the wine becomes overtly grassy. Too brown you get a lignified character.”

Heady with roses, the grenache “comes across seductively on the nose, but the palate reminds you that it’s a wine of substance, with this core of tannin.” The key, he says, is picking before overripeness; grenache’s tendency to overcrop and ripen unevenly makes yield and canopy management crucial.

“I don’t like a lot of alcohol; it takes away from the typicity. Freshness and brightness are what I look for.”

The final wine is the Syrah 2022, from Williams’s own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard, planted in 2000. “I like to think of this wine as straddling a tightrope: plenty of freshness, no excess ripeness, quite lithe and muscular. That’s the style the vineyard lends itself to.”

Viognier may not have worked as a blending partner, but Williams has found success with roussanne, which makes up six per cent of the wine. “I discovered too late in life that in Hermitage a lot of growers harvest a bit of roussanne with their syrah.” Unlike viognier, it brings no overt sweetness or perfume, instead it tempers the syrah’s rusticity, glossing its tannins and adding brightness.

While Williams’s unintentional 25-year experiment makes a compelling case for Rhône varieties in the Cape, a conversation with viticulturist Etienne Terblanche after the tasting adds some perspective.

Grenache says Terblanche is the clearest success story. Against the backdrop of an overall decline in vineyard area, grenache noir has grown from around 50 ha in the early 2000s to some 570–580 ha today, while grenache blanc has increased from roughly 20 ha to 170 ha.

Varieties such as marsanne and roussanne grew from a low base but have largely stabilised over the past decade, while viognier, once planted to around 900–1,000 ha, has since roughly halved.

Mourvèdre is also waning. Terblanche believes commercial viability is part of the equation: varieties such as grenache have enough identity to stand alone, while lesser-known grapes primarily associated with blends can be difficult to communicate and sell. Nor he says are these varieties necessarily a simple answer to climate change. While adapted to warm, dry conditions and useful for increasing varietal diversity, many Rhône whites are naturally more about texture than crisp acidity.

The vineyards need to mature too, young plantings of big-berried varieties such as grenache, carignan and cinsault can take time to come into their own.

What do the next 25 years hold for these grapes? While we wait, to borrow from Williams’s favourite writer, Henry David Thoreau: “Live in each season as it passes; breathe the air, drink the drink, taste the fruit…”.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles. She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert

title: Greg Sherwood MW: Wine, giving and the Pebbles Project
summary:
Over the years, I have read a lot of periodical analyses and critiques about how the South African wine industry is not doing enough when it comes to helping the disadvantaged communities it relies so heavily upon to operate as a successful industry. Some of it may be fact, some of it fiction, but whenever […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Wine, giving and the Pebbles Project appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the years, I have read a lot of periodical analyses and critiques about how the South African wine industry is not doing enough when it comes to helping the disadvantaged communities it relies so heavily upon to operate as a successful industry. Some of it may be fact, some of it fiction, but whenever I am spending longer periods of time in the Cape winelands, I am always curious and enquiring as to what specific projects are successfully operating in the winelands and making a real impact on real peoples’ lives.

On my recent trip to the Cape, I managed to not only spend a week in Stellenbosch judging but also spent an extended time in both Franschhoek and Hemel-en-Aarde. Knowing full well that my time in and around Hermanus would be pulled in a number of directions, I contacted Carolyn Martin of Creation and enquired if there would be any opportunity to do a charity wine dinner for consumers to help raise funds for a local charity.

Carolyn, being the indomitable force that she is, thought it would be a great idea to get some of the local wineries involved in a fine wine dinner to help raise funds for their local branch of Pebbles Project, a charity I had encountered many times before through the very generous fundraising work of ex-Mullineux Wines shareholder Keith Prothero in London, as well as during my time as the Cape Wine Auction’s UK Charity Ambassador, Pebbles Project being a significant beneficiary of the funds raised annually.

Wine farms and social impact

To be honest, I primarily thought that the Pebbles Project was mostly active in and around Stellenbosch but was pleasantly surprised to see how its incredible network had grown to cover great swathes of the Cape’s winelands. The Pebbles Project is a South African non-profit founded in 2004 that works to improve the lives of children and families in the country’s agricultural communities, many of whom are the sons, daughters, and relatives of wine farm workers.

Operating across Somerset West, Stellenbosch, Paarl, Wellington, Citrusdal, and the Hemel-en-Aarde region near Hermanus, Pebbles, as I learnt, currently supports over 1,400 children between the ages of 0 and 18, alongside their families. Its work follows a five-pillar approach covering education, health, nutrition, community development, and child protection through social work programmes, addressing challenges such as poverty, alcohol abuse, and limited access to basic services that are common in farming communities.

As it turns out, one of the organisation’s most notable initiatives happens to be in the Hemel-en-Aarde outside Hermanus. In 2015, Carolyn Martin, co-owner of Creation Wines, approached the Pebbles Project to develop educational facilities for farming families in the Valley.  A local farm owner made available a 10-hectare piece of land, and seed funding from the Cape Wine Auction Trust enabled the opening of an Early Childhood Development and After-School Club centre in 2016. 

The project has since grown substantially: a Rotary Global grant in 2019 funded two additional classrooms, and by 2020 the centre had grown from 62 to 113 learners. Carolyn then explained that when a neighbouring government school closed in 2019 leaving 34 farm children without placements, Pebbles partnered with several donors to open the Pebbles Academy, accommodating learners from Grade 1 to 9. A skills development centre was later added, converting an old onion shed into a facility for 20 young adult learners, in partnership with the Hermanus Rotary Club and international donors.

This is exactly the kind of model that illustrates the strength of cooperation between local wineries and the Pebbles Project, with wine estates providing land, funding, and advocacy, while Pebbles delivers the on-the-ground infrastructure and expertise, together transforming opportunities for generations of farming families. It is projects like this and many others that I believe are simply not talked about enough, with even affluent locals often unaware of the tireless work going on in the background and the ongoing funding demands.

So, on a crisp but very muddy Friday morning, after a long-awaited overnight Walker Bay downpour, I set off with Carolyn to visit the Pebbles Academy in the Valley. Carolyn said we would need at least an hour or so on site, which initially seemed quite long to me. But it was only when I got to the Pebbles Academy and saw its true extent, that I realised what a large and groundbreaking undertaking it really was.

As things turned out, we were there a lot longer than an hour and speaking to all the incredible teachers and children was truly inspiring. The profound effect the opportunities offered by the Academy are having on the children was clear to see. Young lives being changed, improved and enhanced through educational opportunities, a healthy routine and an all-important ‘safe space’ respite away from some of the starker realities of a hard rural upbringing.

A dinner that raised more than R50,000

Heading to the sell-out wine tasting dinner in Hermanus that evening at the Fisherman’s Cottage restaurant, which I was presenting alongside Cape Wine Master Liezl Richards, took on a whole new significance. Beyond the interest and consumer support drummed up by Carolyn Martin, a special mention needs to go to the incredibly generous wineries that provided some sensational wines on the night: Creation, Newton Johnson, Restless River, Crystallum and Thamnus.

Flight one featured four Chardonnays including Thamnus Chardonnay 2023, an embryonically youthful and vibrant wine with more opulent high-tone fruit notes of fresh green honeydew melon, green apple, white pear, and a stony mineral limestone complexity. This was served alongside the excellent Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Chardonnay 2024, sourced from multiple vineyards to reflect the estate in its entirety, showing pear, peach, citrus, and vanilla notes, the palate poised and elegant.

The second pairing featured another blockbuster duo, with Restless River’s incredible Ava Marie Chardonnay 2023 brimming with tension and struck flint minerality along side notes of lemon and herbs, lemon cordial and white peach notes that intermingled with the fabulous stony mineral nuances. This was served with Creation’s top white offering, the Art of Chardonnay 2024, a steely, crystalline expression with incredible tension and focus, wound spring energy and a lemon and lime persistence of note. 2024 is a seriously good vintage in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, despite being a very small harvest.

With three food courses appearing alongside the wine pairings, the first two reds were every bit as exciting as the Chardonnays. The Thamnus Pinot Noir 2022 was layered with sour red plum, black berry, curry leaf and bruised ripe strawberry fruits, the palate imparting a fullness and ripeness with a feel of density and dry extract. The Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Pinot Noir 2024 is also a serious vintage offering, rating an impressive 95/100 from Winemag’s editor, and showing lashings of strawberry, red and black cherry, pink musk and fynbos spice with a rich, succulent palate.

The final red pairing to round out the evening was the always impressive Crystallum Cuvee Cinema Pinot Noir 2024, shining bright with incredibly pure, finessed, supple red and black bramble berry fruits and a pinpoint focus on the palate, served alongside Creation’s beautiful Art of Pinot Noir 2024 flagship red. The aromatics showed incredible intensity with piercing notes of black cherry, black berry and wild strawberry, the palate fruit tempered by a fresh, pure stony minerality and a superb fine-grained texture.

A big thank you has to go to all the wonderful Hermanus residents who supported this Pebbles Project charity dinner so generously, with a notable R1,000 of every ticket sold going directly into the charity’s coffers. Adding to that the funds from two silent auctions of mixed wine rarity cases from the above wineries as well as a generous magnum of Pinot Noir donated by Anthony Hamilton Russell, the evening helped raise well over R50,000.

I cannot take any credit for the hard work in putting the whole evening together, merely for floating the original idea and letting other people run with it, but I was certainly very thankful to have had Carolyn and JC Martin’s generous time and energy as well as the able support of Liezl Richards CWM to help present all the wines on the night. As is so often the case, giving can be so much more rewarding than receiving.

If you would like to donate or assist The Pebbles Project in any way, they can be contacted at: www.pebblesproject.org

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

title: Tim James: Getting out more – two Paarl wineries revisited
summary:
We wine writers don’t get out enough (as I’ve said before and will no doubt say again). Most of us rely too much on what easily comes our way – and too often it’s the same labels again and again. So I was pleased this past month to be prompted to visit a couple of […]

The post Tim James: Getting out more – two Paarl wineries revisited appeared first on winemag.
content:
We wine writers don’t get out enough (as I’ve said before and will no doubt say again). Most of us rely too much on what easily comes our way – and too often it’s the same labels again and again. So I was pleased this past month to be prompted to visit a couple of Paarl producers – both of which I’d been to before, but not for a good few years. Oddly, perhaps, they have a few significant things in common quite beyond being in Paarl (in fact they’re at opposite sides of that now somewhat diminished appellation, with Franschhoek and Wellington both having gained “independence”). And beyond making two really good chenins. Both winemakers are also the owners, both are from other countries, and both are self-taught. There’s probably more, but that’s enough.

Tom Heeremans, who owns Tempel Wines along with his Latvian wife Tatjana Holkina, is one of a handsome contingent of Belgian vignerons in the Cape – I noted well over a dozen at the little Belgian Barrels Trade Festival last year. He has been making the wines himself since 2022 (confidently, but “still learning” and calling on advice when needed). All the wines are pleasingly restrained, and eminently drinkable at well below 14% alcohol.

The small farm is in perhaps the prettiest part of Paarl and provides only some (but a growing proportion) of the grapes for the wines. These are made with a keen eye on the international trade that accounts for some 85% of business – so the rather nice Sorgvry cinsault is being discontinued, as it doesn’t sell well. What does sell, accounting for half of Tempel’s production, is chenin and, less expectedly, tempranillo. Coming off a heritage Wellington vineyard, planted in 1985, the always good chenin, Kattemaai (all the wines have charming Afrikaans-Dutch names), can send different signals, however. Snap up the current 2023 for  a rather delicately charming and fresh version, and the upcoming 2025 for a rather richer and riper one with a touch of pineapple.

Most of the wines bar the attractive, easy-going shiraz-based blend Blydskap sell for R325 off the farm or via the website. Oogwink 2022 is a tasty, pure-fruited and succulently dry Paardeberg shiraz, but the most interesting of the reds to me is the 2023 Tydsaam Tempranillo, the flagship wine at R395. From home-grown and brought-in Wellington fruit – with a touch of Paarl carignan for soft florality, says Tom – it’s destemmed and has some new oak in its 15 months in barrel. Rather fragrant, with a varietal tomato-leaf note, it has some complexity and elegance, the tannins supple. A decent buy, and something pleasingly unusual.

Across the appellation, on the Paarl slopes of the Simonsberg, Kristopher Tillery has been gradually assuming full control of winery and vineyards since his parents (Americans well established in Nigerian agriculture) acquired the farm in 2006. They subsequently enlarged and developed it, while relying on expert consultants. Kristopher, Harvard-trained in economics and sustanable development and now in his early 40s, gradually acquired something more than competence and started to move things in the directions he wanted: towards organic farming in the vineyards and a lighter, fresher and more elegant style in the winery.

Speaking of the radical changes, which lost a few customers who enjoyed the bigger, riper, more flamboyant approach, while gaining new ones, Kristopher says: “I can do it because I want to do it. If I had shareholders it would be different.” The vineyards now have wildlife corridors, making them interspersed with renosterveld, blurring, as Kristopher says, the boundary between “wildness and agriculture”. The farm and winery acquired full organic certification in 2023 and is now a member of the burgeoning Organic Wines South Africa. And the only real struggle he has found is all the paperwork. There are three distinct organic jurisdictions – USA, Europe, and Japan – and they have differing requirements that must be met by imported wines claiming to be organic, meaning that a local organic producer like Noble Hill must meet the most stringent of the demands in all respects.

The results, especially since he took on the winemaking himself a dozen years ago, are impressive. This was very evident in the vertical tasting he put on for me last week showing what has been done over the years on the estate with syrah (which occupies the largest area of the farm’s vineyards). We began with Shiraz 2005, the name changing to Syrah in 2009. The earliest vintages showed ripe power and sweetness, with even the 2005 still drinking well. The years after the arrival of Bernard le Roux in 2010 from Vilafonté show perhaps a great technical mastery, with a little more freshness and succulent balance, while continuing the ripely rich approach. They are all really nice wines for drinking now (but no hurry).

Kristopher’s first vintage in charge of the winemaking was 2014 – he was also by then fully involved in the vineyards, gaining confidence. 2015 is something of a standout in this period, the light-feeling elegance reflecting both earlier picking and a gentler approach in the winery. Then, in 2018, it mutated into Field Atlas (now at last in a more traditional burgundy bottle). Tasting it for Platter Guide a few years later I called it “a winningly bright, perfumed blend of syrah with 7% mourvèdre and 2% viognier. Quite lightly but deftly structured; fresh, flavourful & lively…. Half matured in oak (10% new), half in concrete.”

The 2021 went experimentally a bit too far in the direction of lightness – it’s a touch insubstantial. But things pulled themselves together for the very pleasing 2022, from syrah, mourvèdre, viognier and grenache, that I welcomed a few months back as giving remarkable value at R150 (R149, in fact, on the Noble Hill website). As I said then, it’s handsome, well structured, dry, lipsmacking and with some depth of flavour.

All the Noble Hill wines are well worth exploring and are all good value. But I must just mention again the fine single vineyard chenin – called Simonskop (the priciest wine in the range at R360), bearing the same beautiful painting of that mighty peak as on the Field Atlas label (the other wines’ labels show various old keys). And the Estate Reserve bordeaux-style blend (five varieties, five keys on the label), which I have greatly admired and enjoyed for its modest elegance – the current 2022 shows that character and is another remarkable bargain at R220.

If you need another inducement to visit Noble Hill, if you can, note that the restaurant has been recast from its former focus on Californian-Mexican to a more traditional wine-friendly bistro approach. Though the delicious Chicken Marbella I had (following a possibly even more delicious whipped feta with fresh herbs from the estate garden) is evidence, perhaps, of a continued American touch in the kitchen as well as of very sound cooking. The rebuilding of the restaurant will be finished soon – and other good news is that the end is in sight for the lengthy and deeply troublesome roadworks on what will now be a fine highway between Klapmuts and Simondium.

So all is well at Noble Hill, and Kristopher admits, with great justification I think, looking back at the directed commitment of his work over the past two decades, that “I’m getting to a place where I’m happy”.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

The post Malu Lambert: The Foundry – 25 Years of Rhône in the Cape appeared first on winemag.
content:
There is no better way to explore Rhône varieties in South Africa than through The Foundry’s wines, which set a benchmark for a distinctly Cape interpretation.

Chris Williams of The Foundry.

“The Foundry is 25-years-old this year,” says Chris Williams addressing trade and media on the rooftop of the Melting Pot restaurant. The day is vibrantly hot, the surrounding technicolor buildings of De Waterkant seem to pulse in its brightness. It’s the new vintage-release and the label’s cold viognier is the perfect counterpoint to the weather.

The Foundry “was born very much out of the impact that the Rhône made on me as a young winemaker travelling in 1994”. Established in an old shed at Joostenberg while Williams was at Meerlust, he left in 2020 to focus on the brand full-time.

“It looks like it was a plan,” he says of the five Rhône-style wines we are about to taste. “It wasn’t. The first vintage [2001] was a mishmash of varieties, but the syrah really stood out.” In 2004, he started co-fermenting syrah with viognier. “I liked the gloss, but not the sweetness and overt florals.” Instead, viognier became The Foundry’s second wine and its first white.

“The range evolved organically.” Part of this is the Cape’s suitability. “There are a lot of similarities with the Rhône,” he says, citing granite soils, a Mediterranean climate, windy summers and cold, wet winters. Crucially, says Williams, “they retain their flavour and acidity.”

White masquerading as red

The Viognier 2024 comes from a vineyard six kilometres from False Bay. At 13 per cent alcohol, it is linear, floral and restrained, with less opulence than typical examples. It’s the only wine made entirely in oak: “Terracotta took away too much of the variety’s perfume.”

We move on to the Grenache Blanc 2022 (Williams says it benefits from bottle age). He points out that few places in the world produce a single varietal. “It’s a very Cape style of wine.” By contrast, some examples he’s tasted in southern France and Spain are “actually quite dull”, where the grape is often used for volume and alcohol.

The grapes come primarily from his own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard with the rest from neighbouring grower Willie Mostert. Williams south-facing block ripens about a week later than Mostert’s sunnier, east-facing vineyard. Each vineyard is split into three cuvées: barrel, stainless steel and terracotta. “What makes it so interesting, both red and white, is the mouthfeel,” he posits. “You get this textural pithiness on the mid-palate after the fruit explosion on entry.”

That component is what draws him to the whites. “They’re thick-skinned because they’ve evolved to deal with the harsh climate of the southern Rhône.” The Foundry whites all have varying degrees of grip balanced by fruit and fresh acidity.

With the Roussanne 2024 now in glass, he points out its gold colour, due to its phenolic character. “I’m careful to balance the natural tannin with roussanne’s generous fruit.” Its skin-to-juice ratio yields just 500 litres per tonne from his Voor-Paardeberg vineyard. “Squish a grape and basically a blob of pulp with four seeds comes out.”

The 2024 is perfumed with incense, turmeric, and Chinese five-spice, offset by savouriness and lemony acidity. Fermented equally in terracotta and barrel, it needs oxygen “to really unlock these exotic flavours”.

“I’ve referred to it, usually after a bottle or two, as red wine in drag.” Roussanne, he adds, has incredible ageing potential, noting that his first vintage was 2010 and “that wine is only now fully mature”. One of his favourite wines, he says, is Château de Beaucastel’s Roussanne Vieilles Vignes, which “is just indestructible”.

Fresh and focused reds

“The inclusion of whole bunch is dependent on the stems,” says Williams, answering a question about the Grenache Noir 2022. “Too green, the wine becomes overtly grassy. Too brown you get a lignified character.”

Heady with roses, the grenache “comes across seductively on the nose, but the palate reminds you that it’s a wine of substance, with this core of tannin.” The key, he says, is picking before overripeness; grenache’s tendency to overcrop and ripen unevenly makes yield and canopy management crucial.

“I don’t like a lot of alcohol; it takes away from the typicity. Freshness and brightness are what I look for.”

The final wine is the Syrah 2022, from Williams’s own Voor-Paardeberg vineyard, planted in 2000. “I like to think of this wine as straddling a tightrope: plenty of freshness, no excess ripeness, quite lithe and muscular. That’s the style the vineyard lends itself to.”

Viognier may not have worked as a blending partner, but Williams has found success with roussanne, which makes up six per cent of the wine. “I discovered too late in life that in Hermitage a lot of growers harvest a bit of roussanne with their syrah.” Unlike viognier, it brings no overt sweetness or perfume, instead it tempers the syrah’s rusticity, glossing its tannins and adding brightness.

While Williams’s unintentional 25-year experiment makes a compelling case for Rhône varieties in the Cape, a conversation with viticulturist Etienne Terblanche after the tasting adds some perspective.

Grenache says Terblanche is the clearest success story. Against the backdrop of an overall decline in vineyard area, grenache noir has grown from around 50 ha in the early 2000s to some 570–580 ha today, while grenache blanc has increased from roughly 20 ha to 170 ha.

Varieties such as marsanne and roussanne grew from a low base but have largely stabilised over the past decade, while viognier, once planted to around 900–1,000 ha, has since roughly halved.

Mourvèdre is also waning. Terblanche believes commercial viability is part of the equation: varieties such as grenache have enough identity to stand alone, while lesser-known grapes primarily associated with blends can be difficult to communicate and sell. Nor he says are these varieties necessarily a simple answer to climate change. While adapted to warm, dry conditions and useful for increasing varietal diversity, many Rhône whites are naturally more about texture than crisp acidity.

The vineyards need to mature too, young plantings of big-berried varieties such as grenache, carignan and cinsault can take time to come into their own.

What do the next 25 years hold for these grapes? While we wait, to borrow from Williams’s favourite writer, Henry David Thoreau: “Live in each season as it passes; breathe the air, drink the drink, taste the fruit…”.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles. She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert

title: Greg Sherwood MW: Wine, giving and the Pebbles Project
summary:
Over the years, I have read a lot of periodical analyses and critiques about how the South African wine industry is not doing enough when it comes to helping the disadvantaged communities it relies so heavily upon to operate as a successful industry. Some of it may be fact, some of it fiction, but whenever […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Wine, giving and the Pebbles Project appeared first on winemag.
content:
Over the years, I have read a lot of periodical analyses and critiques about how the South African wine industry is not doing enough when it comes to helping the disadvantaged communities it relies so heavily upon to operate as a successful industry. Some of it may be fact, some of it fiction, but whenever I am spending longer periods of time in the Cape winelands, I am always curious and enquiring as to what specific projects are successfully operating in the winelands and making a real impact on real peoples’ lives.

On my recent trip to the Cape, I managed to not only spend a week in Stellenbosch judging but also spent an extended time in both Franschhoek and Hemel-en-Aarde. Knowing full well that my time in and around Hermanus would be pulled in a number of directions, I contacted Carolyn Martin of Creation and enquired if there would be any opportunity to do a charity wine dinner for consumers to help raise funds for a local charity.

Carolyn, being the indomitable force that she is, thought it would be a great idea to get some of the local wineries involved in a fine wine dinner to help raise funds for their local branch of Pebbles Project, a charity I had encountered many times before through the very generous fundraising work of ex-Mullineux Wines shareholder Keith Prothero in London, as well as during my time as the Cape Wine Auction’s UK Charity Ambassador, Pebbles Project being a significant beneficiary of the funds raised annually.

Wine farms and social impact

To be honest, I primarily thought that the Pebbles Project was mostly active in and around Stellenbosch but was pleasantly surprised to see how its incredible network had grown to cover great swathes of the Cape’s winelands. The Pebbles Project is a South African non-profit founded in 2004 that works to improve the lives of children and families in the country’s agricultural communities, many of whom are the sons, daughters, and relatives of wine farm workers.

Operating across Somerset West, Stellenbosch, Paarl, Wellington, Citrusdal, and the Hemel-en-Aarde region near Hermanus, Pebbles, as I learnt, currently supports over 1,400 children between the ages of 0 and 18, alongside their families. Its work follows a five-pillar approach covering education, health, nutrition, community development, and child protection through social work programmes, addressing challenges such as poverty, alcohol abuse, and limited access to basic services that are common in farming communities.

As it turns out, one of the organisation’s most notable initiatives happens to be in the Hemel-en-Aarde outside Hermanus. In 2015, Carolyn Martin, co-owner of Creation Wines, approached the Pebbles Project to develop educational facilities for farming families in the Valley.  A local farm owner made available a 10-hectare piece of land, and seed funding from the Cape Wine Auction Trust enabled the opening of an Early Childhood Development and After-School Club centre in 2016. 

The project has since grown substantially: a Rotary Global grant in 2019 funded two additional classrooms, and by 2020 the centre had grown from 62 to 113 learners. Carolyn then explained that when a neighbouring government school closed in 2019 leaving 34 farm children without placements, Pebbles partnered with several donors to open the Pebbles Academy, accommodating learners from Grade 1 to 9. A skills development centre was later added, converting an old onion shed into a facility for 20 young adult learners, in partnership with the Hermanus Rotary Club and international donors.

This is exactly the kind of model that illustrates the strength of cooperation between local wineries and the Pebbles Project, with wine estates providing land, funding, and advocacy, while Pebbles delivers the on-the-ground infrastructure and expertise, together transforming opportunities for generations of farming families. It is projects like this and many others that I believe are simply not talked about enough, with even affluent locals often unaware of the tireless work going on in the background and the ongoing funding demands.

So, on a crisp but very muddy Friday morning, after a long-awaited overnight Walker Bay downpour, I set off with Carolyn to visit the Pebbles Academy in the Valley. Carolyn said we would need at least an hour or so on site, which initially seemed quite long to me. But it was only when I got to the Pebbles Academy and saw its true extent, that I realised what a large and groundbreaking undertaking it really was.

As things turned out, we were there a lot longer than an hour and speaking to all the incredible teachers and children was truly inspiring. The profound effect the opportunities offered by the Academy are having on the children was clear to see. Young lives being changed, improved and enhanced through educational opportunities, a healthy routine and an all-important ‘safe space’ respite away from some of the starker realities of a hard rural upbringing.

A dinner that raised more than R50,000

Heading to the sell-out wine tasting dinner in Hermanus that evening at the Fisherman’s Cottage restaurant, which I was presenting alongside Cape Wine Master Liezl Richards, took on a whole new significance. Beyond the interest and consumer support drummed up by Carolyn Martin, a special mention needs to go to the incredibly generous wineries that provided some sensational wines on the night: Creation, Newton Johnson, Restless River, Crystallum and Thamnus.

Flight one featured four Chardonnays including Thamnus Chardonnay 2023, an embryonically youthful and vibrant wine with more opulent high-tone fruit notes of fresh green honeydew melon, green apple, white pear, and a stony mineral limestone complexity. This was served alongside the excellent Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Chardonnay 2024, sourced from multiple vineyards to reflect the estate in its entirety, showing pear, peach, citrus, and vanilla notes, the palate poised and elegant.

The second pairing featured another blockbuster duo, with Restless River’s incredible Ava Marie Chardonnay 2023 brimming with tension and struck flint minerality along side notes of lemon and herbs, lemon cordial and white peach notes that intermingled with the fabulous stony mineral nuances. This was served with Creation’s top white offering, the Art of Chardonnay 2024, a steely, crystalline expression with incredible tension and focus, wound spring energy and a lemon and lime persistence of note. 2024 is a seriously good vintage in the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, despite being a very small harvest.

With three food courses appearing alongside the wine pairings, the first two reds were every bit as exciting as the Chardonnays. The Thamnus Pinot Noir 2022 was layered with sour red plum, black berry, curry leaf and bruised ripe strawberry fruits, the palate imparting a fullness and ripeness with a feel of density and dry extract. The Newton Johnson Family Vineyards Pinot Noir 2024 is also a serious vintage offering, rating an impressive 95/100 from Winemag’s editor, and showing lashings of strawberry, red and black cherry, pink musk and fynbos spice with a rich, succulent palate.

The final red pairing to round out the evening was the always impressive Crystallum Cuvee Cinema Pinot Noir 2024, shining bright with incredibly pure, finessed, supple red and black bramble berry fruits and a pinpoint focus on the palate, served alongside Creation’s beautiful Art of Pinot Noir 2024 flagship red. The aromatics showed incredible intensity with piercing notes of black cherry, black berry and wild strawberry, the palate fruit tempered by a fresh, pure stony minerality and a superb fine-grained texture.

A big thank you has to go to all the wonderful Hermanus residents who supported this Pebbles Project charity dinner so generously, with a notable R1,000 of every ticket sold going directly into the charity’s coffers. Adding to that the funds from two silent auctions of mixed wine rarity cases from the above wineries as well as a generous magnum of Pinot Noir donated by Anthony Hamilton Russell, the evening helped raise well over R50,000.

I cannot take any credit for the hard work in putting the whole evening together, merely for floating the original idea and letting other people run with it, but I was certainly very thankful to have had Carolyn and JC Martin’s generous time and energy as well as the able support of Liezl Richards CWM to help present all the wines on the night. As is so often the case, giving can be so much more rewarding than receiving.

If you would like to donate or assist The Pebbles Project in any way, they can be contacted at: www.pebblesproject.org

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

title: Tim James: Getting out more – two Paarl wineries revisited
summary:
We wine writers don’t get out enough (as I’ve said before and will no doubt say again). Most of us rely too much on what easily comes our way – and too often it’s the same labels again and again. So I was pleased this past month to be prompted to visit a couple of […]

The post Tim James: Getting out more – two Paarl wineries revisited appeared first on winemag.
content:
We wine writers don’t get out enough (as I’ve said before and will no doubt say again). Most of us rely too much on what easily comes our way – and too often it’s the same labels again and again. So I was pleased this past month to be prompted to visit a couple of Paarl producers – both of which I’d been to before, but not for a good few years. Oddly, perhaps, they have a few significant things in common quite beyond being in Paarl (in fact they’re at opposite sides of that now somewhat diminished appellation, with Franschhoek and Wellington both having gained “independence”). And beyond making two really good chenins. Both winemakers are also the owners, both are from other countries, and both are self-taught. There’s probably more, but that’s enough.

Tom Heeremans, who owns Tempel Wines along with his Latvian wife Tatjana Holkina, is one of a handsome contingent of Belgian vignerons in the Cape – I noted well over a dozen at the little Belgian Barrels Trade Festival last year. He has been making the wines himself since 2022 (confidently, but “still learning” and calling on advice when needed). All the wines are pleasingly restrained, and eminently drinkable at well below 14% alcohol.

The small farm is in perhaps the prettiest part of Paarl and provides only some (but a growing proportion) of the grapes for the wines. These are made with a keen eye on the international trade that accounts for some 85% of business – so the rather nice Sorgvry cinsault is being discontinued, as it doesn’t sell well. What does sell, accounting for half of Tempel’s production, is chenin and, less expectedly, tempranillo. Coming off a heritage Wellington vineyard, planted in 1985, the always good chenin, Kattemaai (all the wines have charming Afrikaans-Dutch names), can send different signals, however. Snap up the current 2023 for  a rather delicately charming and fresh version, and the upcoming 2025 for a rather richer and riper one with a touch of pineapple.

Most of the wines bar the attractive, easy-going shiraz-based blend Blydskap sell for R325 off the farm or via the website. Oogwink 2022 is a tasty, pure-fruited and succulently dry Paardeberg shiraz, but the most interesting of the reds to me is the 2023 Tydsaam Tempranillo, the flagship wine at R395. From home-grown and brought-in Wellington fruit – with a touch of Paarl carignan for soft florality, says Tom – it’s destemmed and has some new oak in its 15 months in barrel. Rather fragrant, with a varietal tomato-leaf note, it has some complexity and elegance, the tannins supple. A decent buy, and something pleasingly unusual.

Across the appellation, on the Paarl slopes of the Simonsberg, Kristopher Tillery has been gradually assuming full control of winery and vineyards since his parents (Americans well established in Nigerian agriculture) acquired the farm in 2006. They subsequently enlarged and developed it, while relying on expert consultants. Kristopher, Harvard-trained in economics and sustanable development and now in his early 40s, gradually acquired something more than competence and started to move things in the directions he wanted: towards organic farming in the vineyards and a lighter, fresher and more elegant style in the winery.

Speaking of the radical changes, which lost a few customers who enjoyed the bigger, riper, more flamboyant approach, while gaining new ones, Kristopher says: “I can do it because I want to do it. If I had shareholders it would be different.” The vineyards now have wildlife corridors, making them interspersed with renosterveld, blurring, as Kristopher says, the boundary between “wildness and agriculture”. The farm and winery acquired full organic certification in 2023 and is now a member of the burgeoning Organic Wines South Africa. And the only real struggle he has found is all the paperwork. There are three distinct organic jurisdictions – USA, Europe, and Japan – and they have differing requirements that must be met by imported wines claiming to be organic, meaning that a local organic producer like Noble Hill must meet the most stringent of the demands in all respects.

The results, especially since he took on the winemaking himself a dozen years ago, are impressive. This was very evident in the vertical tasting he put on for me last week showing what has been done over the years on the estate with syrah (which occupies the largest area of the farm’s vineyards). We began with Shiraz 2005, the name changing to Syrah in 2009. The earliest vintages showed ripe power and sweetness, with even the 2005 still drinking well. The years after the arrival of Bernard le Roux in 2010 from Vilafonté show perhaps a great technical mastery, with a little more freshness and succulent balance, while continuing the ripely rich approach. They are all really nice wines for drinking now (but no hurry).

Kristopher’s first vintage in charge of the winemaking was 2014 – he was also by then fully involved in the vineyards, gaining confidence. 2015 is something of a standout in this period, the light-feeling elegance reflecting both earlier picking and a gentler approach in the winery. Then, in 2018, it mutated into Field Atlas (now at last in a more traditional burgundy bottle). Tasting it for Platter Guide a few years later I called it “a winningly bright, perfumed blend of syrah with 7% mourvèdre and 2% viognier. Quite lightly but deftly structured; fresh, flavourful & lively…. Half matured in oak (10% new), half in concrete.”

The 2021 went experimentally a bit too far in the direction of lightness – it’s a touch insubstantial. But things pulled themselves together for the very pleasing 2022, from syrah, mourvèdre, viognier and grenache, that I welcomed a few months back as giving remarkable value at R150 (R149, in fact, on the Noble Hill website). As I said then, it’s handsome, well structured, dry, lipsmacking and with some depth of flavour.

All the Noble Hill wines are well worth exploring and are all good value. But I must just mention again the fine single vineyard chenin – called Simonskop (the priciest wine in the range at R360), bearing the same beautiful painting of that mighty peak as on the Field Atlas label (the other wines’ labels show various old keys). And the Estate Reserve bordeaux-style blend (five varieties, five keys on the label), which I have greatly admired and enjoyed for its modest elegance – the current 2022 shows that character and is another remarkable bargain at R220.

If you need another inducement to visit Noble Hill, if you can, note that the restaurant has been recast from its former focus on Californian-Mexican to a more traditional wine-friendly bistro approach. Though the delicious Chicken Marbella I had (following a possibly even more delicious whipped feta with fresh herbs from the estate garden) is evidence, perhaps, of a continued American touch in the kitchen as well as of very sound cooking. The rebuilding of the restaurant will be finished soon – and other good news is that the end is in sight for the lengthy and deeply troublesome roadworks on what will now be a fine highway between Klapmuts and Simondium.

So all is well at Noble Hill, and Kristopher admits, with great justification I think, looking back at the directed commitment of his work over the past two decades, that “I’m getting to a place where I’m happy”.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.
